1366.title: Coptic and Ge'ez Catholics
1366.hook: Egypt, Ethiopia and Eritrea have their own Catholic churches
1366.howItsDone: Coptic Catholics celebrate the liturgy in the Alexandrian tradition in Coptic and Arabic; Ethiopian and Eritrean Catholics celebrate it in the Ge'ez tradition, with Ge'ez and local languages, sharing music, fasts and feasts with their Orthodox neighbors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Chaldeans of Iraq, who still pray in Syriac, a form of Aramaic. Your line was the language of jesus.

An official from Ethiopia is riding home in a chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah aloud, and he can't make sense of it. A stranger runs alongside and asks whether he understands what he's reading. How can I, the man says, unless someone shows me? That stranger is Philip, and the story is in the Acts of the Apostles. By the end of the chapter, the man has asked to be baptized at water beside the road, and he goes on his way rejoicing. Africa is already in the story, in the New Testament itself.
screen: `A CHARIOT, AND ISAIAH ALOUD.` → `HOW CAN I, UNLESS SOMEONE SHOWS ME?` → `AFRICA, FROM THE OPENING PAGES.`

segments.voice: Egypt comes first. Matthew's Gospel says an angel told Joseph, in the Douay-Rheims, "Arise, and take the child and his mother, and fly into Egypt." So the Holy Family were refugees in Egypt. Egyptian Christians, called Copts, treasure that, and tradition says the evangelist Mark later brought the Gospel to Alexandria. Beside the Coptic Orthodox Church stands a smaller community, the Coptic Catholic Church, which prays in the same Coptic tradition, using Coptic and Arabic, in communion with Rome. Then Ethiopia and Eritrea. Acts calls the man in the chariot "a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch," a royal treasurer. Ethiopian Christians honor him, and their own tradition tells of the faith arriving at the royal court long ago. Their ancient church language is Ge'ez, with its own script, still used in prayer though no longer spoken at home. Here too there is an ancient Orthodox church, and alongside it two Catholic churches, the Ethiopian Catholic Church and the Eritrean Catholic Church, both praying in the Ge'ez tradition. Drums and sistrums in the liturgy. Long fasts. White shawls. Priests carrying hand crosses that people kiss for a blessing. Last, those Orthodox neighbors. These Catholic churches share a great deal with them: the language, the music, the saints, the fasts. What differs is communion with the bishop of Rome. The Catholic Church speaks of these Orthodox churches with deep respect, and prays for full unity, not for one to swallow the other.
screen: `FLY INTO EGYPT.` · `COPTIC CATHOLICS, ON THE NILE.` · `GE'EZ: THE PRAYER LANGUAGE OF ETHIOPIA.` · `SHARING NEARLY EVERYTHING WITH THE ORTHODOX.` · then, large: `A MAN OF ETHIOPIA, AN EUNUCH.`

segments.voice: Picture the Horn of Africa: highlands and dry plains, a church cut into rock, a market at noon, a family on the move because of drought or war. Then picture the man in the chariot, reading and puzzled, and the stranger who ran to help him. If you pray, pray for Ethiopia, Eritrea and their neighbors, and for Egypt too; if you don't, hold the people of that region in your attention, with respect.
Coptic and Ge'ez Catholics. The Eastern Catholic churches of Egypt, Ethiopia and Eritrea, sharing the ancient traditions of their Orthodox neighbors and in communion with Rome. Today's word.
Your line: africa's ancient churches. How can I, the man asked, unless someone shows me? Rest well.

1367.title: The Armenian Catholics
1367.hook: heirs of the first nation to adopt Christianity
1367.howItsDone: Armenian Catholics celebrate the Armenian Divine Liturgy in Classical Armenian, sharing its music, saints and feasts with the Armenian Apostolic Church, and honor Saint Gregory the Illuminator as the one who brought the faith to Armenia.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Coptic and Ge'ez Catholics: Egypt, Ethiopia and Eritrea, and a man in a chariot reading Isaiah. Your line was africa's ancient churches.

"The ark rested … upon the mountains of Armenia." That's Genesis, in the Douay-Rheims, at the end of the flood. Noah's boat comes to rest, and the name on the map is Armenia. Armenians call a great snow-capped mountain on their horizon Ararat, and tradition ties it to that story. But the story at the center of Armenian Christianity comes much later, and it begins in a pit: a man thrown into a deep hole by a king, and left there to die.
screen: `THE MOUNTAINS OF ARMENIA.` → `ARARAT ON THE HORIZON.` → `A MAN IN A PIT.`

segments.voice: Armenian tradition tells of Gregory, a Christian who served at the royal court and refused to worship the old gods. The king had him tortured and thrown into a pit, where, the story goes, he survived for years, fed in secret by a kind woman. Then the king fell gravely ill, and no one could heal him. Gregory was brought up out of the pit, prayed over the king, and the king was healed and baptized. Armenians call him Saint Gregory the Illuminator, the one who brought light. Then the claim in today's line. Armenians say that when their king was baptized, the kingdom became Christian with him, so they speak of Armenia as the first nation to adopt Christianity. It's a claim at the heart of how Armenians see themselves; historians discuss the details, and others make claims of their own. Then the alphabet. Tradition says a monk named Mesrop created the Armenian letters so the Bible could be read in Armenian, and the script is still in use today. A people with their own scripture in their own letters. Last, the Armenian Catholics. The ancient church of the Armenian people is the Armenian Apostolic Church. Some Armenian communities came into communion with Rome and became the Armenian Catholic Church, praying the same Armenian liturgy, with the same saints, the same music, the same letters. Armenians have known great suffering, and their churches, Apostolic and Catholic, have gone into exile together and prayed for the same dead.
screen: `GREGORY IN THE PIT.` · `THE KING HEALED AND BAPTIZED.` · `ARMENIANS SAY: THE FIRST NATION.` · `THEIR OWN LETTERS, THEIR OWN LITURGY.` · then, large: `UPON THE MOUNTAINS OF ARMENIA.`

segments.voice: Picture a stone church on a high plateau, a mountain white against the sky, an old woman lighting a thin candle in sand, and families scattered far from those mountains who still teach their children the letters. If you pray, pray for Armenia and its people, near and far. If you don't, simply honor them: a people who kept a faith, a liturgy and an alphabet through a great deal.

The Armenian Catholics. Armenians in communion with Rome who pray the ancient Armenian liturgy and honor Saint Gregory the Illuminator, heirs of what Armenians call the first Christian nation. Today's word.
Your line: the first nation. A story that began in a pit ended with a light-bringer. I'll be here tomorrow.

1368.title: Theosis (CCC 460)
1368.hook: the Son of God became man so that we might share his divinity
1368.howItsDone: Eastern Catholics, like the Orthodox, speak of theosis as the goal of the Christian life; Latin Catholics usually speak of grace and sharing in the divine life, and the Catechism (CCC 460) presents both together.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Armenian Catholics, and Gregory, brought up from the pit to pray over the king who put him there. Your line was the first nation.

Ask a room of churchgoers why God became man, and the answers come quickly. To forgive our sins. To show us the way. To die for us. All of those are in the Catechism. But in one short paragraph, number four hundred sixty, it gives a reason that's easy to read past: the Word became flesh to make us partakers of the divine nature. Not just forgiven. Brought into God's own life. The Eastern churches we've been visiting have a word for this, and they treasure it.
screen: `TO FORGIVE, TO SHOW THE WAY.` → `AND ONE MORE REASON.` → `PARTAKERS OF THE DIVINE NATURE.`

segments.voice: Underneath the paragraph is a line from scripture. The Second Letter of Peter says, in the Douay-Rheims, that God has given us most great and precious promises, "that by these you may be made partakers of the divine nature." A partaker is someone who has a share. Not an owner. A sharer. The Catechism calls saints as witnesses: Saint Irenaeus, Saint Athanasius and Saint Thomas Aquinas, West and East side by side, all saying the same startling thing. Athanasius's line, in an old English translation, is short enough to memorize: "For He was made man that we might be made God." That line can be heard wrong. It doesn't mean people become a second God, or stop being creatures, or dissolve into God like sugar in tea. Eastern writers explain it with a picture: iron left in a fire. It glows, it burns, it gives off heat and light, and it's still iron. The fire is the fire's own; the iron shares it. That's theosis: being drawn into God's life by grace, while remaining yourself, a creature, a person. It sheds light on what we've seen these past days. The icons show saints already shining with that light. The liturgy is heaven touching earth. Babies receive communion, and God's life is offered from the start. Catholics in the West tend to say grace, sanctification, or sharing in the divine life. Catholics in the East say theosis. The Catechism puts both vocabularies on one page.
screen: `PARTAKERS OF THE DIVINE NATURE.` · `IRENAEUS, ATHANASIUS, AQUINAS.` · `IRON IN THE FIRE: GLOWING, STILL IRON.` · `ONE PAGE, TWO VOCABULARIES.` · then, large: `HE WAS MADE MAN THAT WE MIGHT BE MADE GOD.`

segments.voice: Let the line come back slowly: he was made man that we might be made God. Don't analyze it; notice which word catches, man, made, God, we, and stay with that one word for a few breaths, like iron in the fire, still iron, glowing. If you pray, simply rest in the line, words the Church has kept; if you don't, let it be a sentence someone believed enough to stake a life on, and keep it company.
Theosis. The Eastern Christian word for being drawn into God's own life by grace, made partakers of the divine nature while remaining creatures. Today's word.

1369.title: Great Lent
1369.hook: Eastern Lent begins on Clean Monday with stricter fasting
1369.howItsDone: In the Byzantine Catholic churches, Great Lent begins on Clean Monday after Forgiveness Sunday vespers, where people ask one another's forgiveness; the traditional fast sets aside meat and dairy, and the Prayer of Saint Ephrem is said with prostrations on Lenten weekdays.

segments.voice: Yesterday, theosis: drawn into God's life by grace, like iron glowing in fire, still iron. Your line was made sharers.

Sunday evening, in a Byzantine Catholic church. Vespers has just ended, and the priest steps down, bows to the people, and asks their forgiveness. Then the people line up and bow to each other, one by one. Forgive me, a sinner. God forgives, the other answers. A teenager bows to her grandmother. Two men who haven't spoken in months end up face to face in the line. The next morning there are no ashes, no Wednesday. Lent has simply begun, on a Monday, with a name that sounds like a fresh sheet of paper.
screen: `THE PRIEST BOWS TO THE PEOPLE.` → `FORGIVE ME. GOD FORGIVES.` → `LENT BEGINS ON A MONDAY.`

segments.voice: Eastern Christians call it Great Lent, and its first day Clean Monday. The idea is in Isaiah, in the Douay-Rheims: "Wash yourselves, be clean." Not a scrubbed kitchen, though some families do clean house. A clean heart, after a night of forgiving and being forgiven. Then the fast. Western Catholics today fast on a few set days of Lent and abstain from meat on its Fridays. The traditional Byzantine fast asks more: through the whole season, meat and dairy are set aside, and on Clean Monday some people eat very little at all. Eastern Catholic churches differ in how strictly they keep it now, and people are often given gentler rules for health or work. Eastern teachers say the point was never the menu. It's freedom: a body that learns it can say no to a craving can learn to say yes to God. In Byzantine churches, a short prayer attributed to Saint Ephrem the Syrian is said on weekdays of Lent with deep bows. It asks God to take away laziness, discouragement, the lust for power and idle talk, and to give chastity, humility, patience and love, and the grace to see one's own faults and not judge a brother. Last, Jesus's own instruction about fasting, which East and West both read: "But thou, when thou fastest anoint thy head, and wash thy face." No sour face. No show. Fasting done cleanly, from Clean Monday to the feast.
screen: `WASH YOURSELVES, BE CLEAN.` · `A LONGER, STRICTER FAST.` · `THE PRAYER OF SAINT EPHREM.` · `NO SOUR FACE, NO SHOW.` · then, large: `ANOINT THY HEAD, AND WASH THY FACE.`

segments.voice: Think of your next meal, or tomorrow's, and picture it plainer: bread and soup, rice and beans, one dish instead of three, eaten slowly without the phone. Then notice what that small freedom might make room for: an apology, a phone call, a moment of prayer, money to give away. If you pray, offer the plain meal for someone who has too little; if you don't, let it be a small act of attention.
Great Lent. The Eastern season of fasting before Pascha, beginning on Clean Monday, after a Sunday of mutual forgiveness, with a longer and stricter fast. Today's word.

1370.title: Pascha
1370.hook: Christ is risen! Truly he is risen!
1370.howItsDone: Eastern Catholics celebrate Pascha at a night service with candles, a procession around the church and the repeated greeting "Christ is risen! Truly he is risen!", and use the greeting in place of hello throughout the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Great Lent, which begins on a Monday after everyone bows and asks forgiveness. Your line was clean monday.

Near midnight, and the church is dark. Not dim. Dark. Everyone is holding an unlit candle. Then the priest comes out from behind the icon screen holding a single flame, and the light starts to travel, his candle to the first person's, theirs to the next, until the whole room is gold and flickering. The people follow him outside and walk around the church in the night air, singing. At the closed front doors, the priest calls out a short greeting, and the crowd shouts back an answer, loud enough to wake the street. Then the doors open, and Lent is over.
screen: `A DARK CHURCH, ONE FLAME.` → `AROUND THE CHURCH, SINGING.` → `THE DOORS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Pascha is what Eastern Christians call Easter. Paul ties it straight to the Passover lamb: in the Douay-Rheims, "For Christ our pasch is sacrificed." The pasch is the Passover. Easter, for these churches, is the new Passover, the night God leads his people from death into life. Then the greeting. Christ is risen! Truly he is risen! It's said in Greek, Arabic, Ukrainian, Malayalam, Ge'ez, the languages of the churches we've visited. The answer isn't decoration. It echoes the first Easter evening in Luke, when the disciples tell each other, "The Lord is risen indeed." Indeed. Truly. It's a witness, said back. And people keep saying it, as a hello and a goodbye, through the Easter season. Then the hymn they sing outside the doors, which the Byzantine churches repeat over and over: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and giving life to those in the tombs. Last, a sermon read aloud at the midnight liturgy, attributed to Saint John Chrysostom. It invites everyone to the feast: those who fasted the whole of Lent, those who came at the last hour, and those who didn't fast at all. Nobody should go away hungry, it says. Nobody should mourn their failings, because forgiveness has risen from the tomb. After a strict Lent, that's not the moment to check who kept the rules. The table is set for all.
screen: `CHRIST OUR PASCH: THE NEW PASSOVER.` · `TRULY HE IS RISEN: A WITNESS SAID BACK.` · `TRAMPLING DOWN DEATH BY DEATH.` · `THE TABLE IS SET FOR ALL.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS RISEN INDEED.`

segments.voice: Say the greeting quietly a few times, Christ is risen, truly he is risen, letting the second line come a little stronger, the way a crowd answers. Picture someone you could greet this way at Easter, a friend, a grandparent, someone in a parish hall, and their face as they answer. If you pray, the greeting itself can be your prayer; if you don't, hold it as a sentence shouted at midnight in many languages, and notice how it lands.
Pascha. The Eastern name for Easter, the new Passover, the feast of Christ's resurrection, opened at midnight with candles and a shouted greeting. Today's word.
Your line: truly he is risen. It's a witness, said back a little stronger. See you tomorrow.

1371.title: Toward unity
1371.hook: Catholics and Orthodox continue dialogue and marked 1,700 years since Nicaea in 2025
1371.howItsDone: The Catholic Church takes part in official theological dialogue with the Orthodox churches, and popes and patriarchs meet, pray together and exchange delegations on their churches' patronal feasts; Catholics pray for Christian unity, including during the Week of Prayer for Christian Unity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pascha: a dark church, one flame, and a greeting shouted back at the doors. Your line was truly he is risen.

Two old men in long robes walk toward each other in Jerusalem. One is the bishop of Rome, the other the patriarch of Constantinople. Their churches have been divided a long time, with excommunications on the books, hurt on both sides, and a long habit of not speaking. They don't sign a treaty or settle a single doctrine. They embrace, and exchange a kiss of peace, the way the liturgy does it. A small gesture. Afterward, the old excommunications are lifted, and the two churches begin talking in earnest.
screen: `TWO OLD MEN IN JERUSALEM.` → `NO TREATY. AN EMBRACE.` → `THE OLD EXCOMMUNICATIONS LIFTED.`

segments.voice: At the supper before his arrest, in John's Gospel, Jesus prays for his followers, in the Douay-Rheims, "That they all may be one, as thou, Father, in me, and I in thee." The Catholic Church takes that prayer as a task, not a wish. Catholics and Orthodox already share a great deal: the same sacraments, bishops in succession from the apostles, the Creed of Nicaea, the early councils, the Mother of God, the saints, the icons. They have marked the anniversary of the Council of Nicaea together, remembering a creed they both still pray. What divides them is real too, above all the role of the bishop of Rome, and it is worked on slowly, in official dialogue, by theologians from both sides. Then the honest part. Eastern Catholic churches speak of themselves as a sign that East and West can share one communion. Some Orthodox see them differently, as a wound from the past. Catholic and Orthodox theologians have said together that bringing communities over one by one is not the path to unity today. Both views are held by people of good faith. Last, what's in reach now. Paul writes, "One Lord, one faith, one baptism." Catholics and Orthodox can pray for each other, visit each other, learn each other's hymns, and greet each other at Pascha with the same words. The day of full communion isn't here. But the embrace came first, before any agreement, and the road starts there.

1372.title: What a devotion is
1372.hook: a personal practice that helps faith, beneath the liturgy
1372.howItsDone: Catholics take part in the Church's shared liturgy, above all the Mass, and alongside it some keep personal devotions such as the rosary, novenas, the Stations of the Cross or wearing a blessed medal; these are encouraged but never required.

segments.voice: Yesterday, toward unity: Catholics and Orthodox still talking across an old split. Your line was one day together.

Over coffee, a man preparing to become Catholic asks his sponsor a nervous question. Do I have to pray the rosary? The mercy prayer at three? A scapular? The nine-day things? She laughs and says no, none of them. Then she confuses him more: she keeps all of them, and wouldn't give one up. Both answers are true, and the space between them is today's word. For the coming weeks this path walks through the practices that fill Catholic kitchens, purses and parish bulletins.
screen: `DO I HAVE TO?` → `NO.` → `BUT SHE KEEPS ALL OF THEM.`

segments.voice: The Second Vatican Council, in its document on the liturgy, calls the liturgy the summit the Church's life climbs toward and the fountain its strength flows from. The Mass and the sacraments are the Church's common prayer, the same for everyone. Acts pictures that shared life, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." Around that center grows a garden of other practices: the rosary, the Stations of the Cross, novenas, medals, a picture of the Sacred Heart in the kitchen. The Church calls these devotions, or popular piety. The council commends them warmly, with a condition: they should fit the seasons of the Church's year, flow from the liturgy, and lead people back to it. A devotion is a side path that always rejoins the main road. It's chosen, and it often arrives through a person: a grandmother's rosary, a saint met in a book, a prayer card from a funeral. Luke shows Mary doing this after the shepherds leave: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." Nobody assigned her that. Popular piety, the Catechism says, is a real richness that needs the Church's guidance and discernment to stay rooted in the faith. A devotion helps when it carries a person toward God and toward other people. It stops helping when it turns into a box to tick, or a way of bargaining. Optional doesn't mean minor. Some people carry one small practice through an illness or a long night in a hospital corridor.
screen: `THE LITURGY: SUMMIT AND FOUNTAIN.` · `DEVOTIONS GROW AROUND IT.` · `CHOSEN, OFTEN HANDED ON.` · `GUIDED, SO IT LEADS BACK.` · then, large: `MARY KEPT ALL THESE WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let a few devotions pass through your mind: beads in a pocket, a quiet minute at three, a candle before an image, nine days of praying for one person, a medal on a chain. Notice which you lean toward, and choose that one to try once, soon. If you pray, offer that choice to God; if you don't, hold it as something to understand from the inside.
